title: Relative clauses 4: extra information clauses (1)
subtitle: My brother Ben, who lives in Hong Kong, ...
summary: Tell the two types of relative clause apart: the kind that says which person or thing you mean, and the kind that only adds extra information and needs commas.

lesson.heading: Two types of relative clause

left.label: Type 1: which one?
left.text: The clause tells us which person or thing the speaker means. No commas.
examples: The woman **who lives next door to me** is a doctor.
Grace works for a company **that makes furniture**.
We stayed at the hotel **(that) you recommended**.

right.label: Type 2: extra information
right.text: We already know which person or thing is meant. The clause just adds extra information, and we use commas.
examples: My brother Ben, **who lives in Hong Kong**, is an architect.
Anna told me about her new job, **which she's enjoying a lot**.
We stayed at the Park Hotel, **which a friend of ours recommended**.

lesson.note: In Type 2 we already know who or what is meant: 'My brother Ben', 'Anna's new job', 'the Park Hotel'.

lesson.heading: Type 1: no commas
lesson.text: In Type 1 the relative clause is essential - without it we would not know which person or thing is meant. We do not use commas.

examples.text: We know a lot of people **who live in London**.
The doctor **who examined me** couldn't find anything wrong.
The office **I'm using** at the moment is very small.

lesson.heading: In Type 2 you cannot use that
lesson.text: In both types we use **who** for people and **which** for things. But in Type 2 you cannot use **that**, and you cannot leave who/which out.

examples.text: John, **who speaks** French and Italian, works as a tour guide.
examples.wrong: John, that speaks French and Italian

examples.text: We stayed at the Park Hotel, **which** a friend of ours recommended.
examples.note: which cannot be left out here

examples.text: Type 1: Do you know anyone **who/that speaks** French and Italian?
Type 1: We stayed at the hotel **(that/which) you recommended**.

lesson.heading: whom in Type 2
lesson.text: In Type 2 clauses you can use **whom** for people when it is the object. In Type 1 we do not often use whom.

examples.text: This morning I met Chris, **who I hadn't seen** for ages.
This morning I met Chris, **whom I hadn't seen** for ages.
Kate's husband, **who I've never met**, is an airline pilot.

lesson.heading: whose and where in both types
lesson.text: **Whose** and **where** work in Type 1 and Type 2 clauses in the same way. Only the commas change.

examples.text: Type 1: We helped some people **whose car had broken down**.
Type 2: Lisa, **whose car had broken down**, was in a very bad mood.
Type 1: What's the name of the place **where you went on holiday**?
Type 2: Kate has just been to Sweden, **where her daughter lives**.

lesson.text: Read the sentence without the relative clause. If it still tells you exactly who or what is meant, the clause is extra information and needs commas.

exercises.prompt: My brother Ben, ___ lives in Hong Kong, is an architect.
exercises.explanation: This is an extra information clause about a person, and we cannot use that in this type.

exercises.prompt: Anna told me about her new job, ___ she's enjoying a lot.
exercises.explanation: Extra information about a thing takes which - never that or what.

exercises.statement: The office I'm using at the moment is very small.
exercises.explanation: Correct. This clause tells us which office, so there are no commas and the relative pronoun can be left out.

exercises.statement: My office that is on the second floor is very small.
exercises.explanation: My office, which is on the second floor, is very small. We already know which office is meant, so we need commas and which.

exercises.prompt: We drove to the airport, ___ not far from the city.
exercises.explanation: Extra information about the airport, so we use which after a comma.

exercises.prompt: Lisa is away from home a lot. Her job involves a lot of travelling. Lisa, ___ job involves a lot of travelling, is away from home a lot.
exercises.explanation: Whose works in extra information clauses too: her job involves a lot of travelling.

exercises.prompt: Catherine is very friendly and she lives next door to us. Make one sentence.
exercises.answer: Catherine, who lives next door to us, is very friendly
exercises.explanation: We already know who Catherine is, so the clause is extra information between commas.

exercises.prompt: Kate has just been to Sweden, ___ her daughter lives.
exercises.explanation: Where is used for places in both types of relative clause.

exercises.statement: Sarah's father that used to be in the army now works for a TV company.
exercises.explanation: Sarah's father, who used to be in the army, now works for a TV company. We know which person is meant, so we need commas and who.

exercises.prompt: Our teacher was very kind, but I have forgotten her name. Our teacher, ___ name I have forgotten, was very kind.
exercises.explanation: Whose replaces her: I have forgotten her name.

exercises.prompt: Kate's husband, ___ I have never met, is an airline pilot.
exercises.explanation: In an extra information clause both who and whom are possible for the object - but not that.

exercises.prompt: The commas have been removed. Does the relative clause say which person or thing is meant, or does it only add extra information?

items.text: My brother Ben who lives in Hong Kong is an architect.
The woman who lives next door to me is a doctor.
Anna told me about her new job which she's enjoying a lot.
We know a lot of people who live in London.
The sun which is one of millions of stars provides us with heat and light.
The doctor who examined me couldn't find anything wrong.
